levels.title: Ledger basics
levels.blurb: What the XRP Ledger is, how it agrees, and what accounts, transactions and tokens are.

levels.title: Who is in control
levels.blurb: What issuers can still do, who can sign for an account, NFT rights, and how the rules change.

levels.title: Markets and payments
levels.blurb: Order books, AMM pools, partial payments, and checking that an invoice was really paid.

levels.title: NOSHASHI at work
levels.blurb: Compliance words, how the app reads the ledger, verdicts and receipts, every screen, and teams.

levels.title: Keeping people safe
levels.blurb: Protecting an account, what to do after a theft, getting stuck XRP back, and protecting customers.

lessons.title: One shared record
goals: I can say what the XRP Ledger is in one sentence.
I can explain what makes a ledger validated, and why that matters.

cards.title: A public record of who owns what
cards.text: The XRP Ledger (XRPL) is a public database that has run since 2012. Thousands of servers keep identical copies. Anyone can read it. Nobody, not even the people who built it, can quietly change it.

cards.title: A new page every few seconds
cards.text: Every 3 to 5 seconds the network makes a new ledger: a snapshot of every account and balance. Each ledger gets a number called its ledger index. The number only goes up. It is now past 107 million.

cards.title: Think of it like
cards.text: A notebook that thousands of accountants keep at the same time. Every few seconds they compare their newest page. When 80% of the ones you trust wrote the same page, it is glued into the book forever.

cards.title: Validated means final
cards.text: Special servers called validators vote. When at least 80% of the validators a server trusts agree, the ledger is validated. After that it can never be reversed or edited. NOSHASHI only reads validated ledgers.

cards.title: Why NOSHASHI shows a ledger number
cards.text: Every NOSHASHI result says which ledger it was read at, for example "ledger 107,207,971". Because that ledger can never change, anyone can ask any server for the same ledger later and check the reading.

lessons.keyIdea: Validated means final. A ledger index is a timestamp nobody can argue with.

quiz.question: How often does the XRP Ledger make a new ledger?
quiz.why: A new ledger closes every 3 to 5 seconds, each with a higher ledger index.

quiz.question: What makes a ledger validated?
options: At least 80% of the validators a server trusts agreed on it
It is more than one day old
quiz.why: Validators vote. Once 80% of a server's trusted list agree, the ledger is validated and final.

quiz.question: Why does every NOSHASHI result carry a ledger index?
options: So anyone can re-check the reading against the same, unchangeable ledger
Because it is the price of the reading
quiz.why: A validated ledger never changes, so the same ledger index always gives the same facts.

lessons.title: Accounts, keys and reserves
goals: I can recognise an XRPL address.
I can explain why the secret key matters and why some XRP cannot be spent.

cards.title: An address starts with r
cards.text: An account holds XRP and tokens. Its address starts with a lower-case r and is 25 to 35 characters long. Example: Bitstamp's USD issuer, rvYAfWj5gh67oV6fW32ZzP3Aw4Eubs59B. Addresses never contain 0, O, I or l.

cards.title: Whoever holds the secret owns the account
cards.text: A secret (often starting with s) controls the account. Anyone who has it can move everything. Never share it, never type it into a website. NOSHASHI never asks for it: it only reads public data.

cards.title: The reserve
cards.text: Every account keeps some XRP locked so the shared ledger does not fill with junk: 1 XRP to exist, plus 0.2 XRP for each thing it owns, like a trust line or an offer. Locked XRP cannot be spent.

cards.title: Balance is not the same as spendable
cards.text: An account with 10 XRP that owns 5 objects has 1 + 5 × 0.2 = 2 XRP locked. Only 8 XRP can move. NOSHASHI shows both numbers so you never mistake one for the other.

cards.title: A common mistake
cards.text: An account's Sequence number is not how many transactions it made. It starts near the ledger index when the account was created, so a big number can mean a young account.

lessons.keyIdea: Whoever holds the key owns the account. Balance minus reserve is what can actually move.

quiz.question: Which of these is an XRPL address?
quiz.why: Addresses start with r. The second is a ledger index, and the third is a 64-character transaction hash. All three are real, from lessons in this course.

quiz.question: An account has 10 XRP and owns 5 objects. About how much can it spend?
quiz.why: 1 XRP base reserve plus 5 × 0.2 XRP owner reserve locks 2 XRP, leaving 8.

quiz.question: Does NOSHASHI ever need your secret key?
options: No, it only reads public data
quiz.why: NOSHASHI never asks for a secret, never signs and never moves money.

lessons.title: Transactions and what results mean
goals: I can name a few transaction types.
I can read a result code and know whether it is final.

cards.title: Every change is a transaction
cards.text: A transaction is a signed instruction. Payment sends value. OfferCreate places a trade. TrustSet opens a trust line. AccountSet changes a setting. Each one pays a tiny fee in XRP that is destroyed, not paid to anyone.

cards.title: Only validated results count
cards.text: When a transaction is first submitted, the server gives a tentative result. It becomes final only when it is in a validated ledger. The final result is stored in the transaction's metadata.

cards.title: Reading the result code
cards.text: tesSUCCESS: it worked. tec…: it failed but was recorded, and the fee was charged. tef, tel, tem or ter: it was not applied at all, and no fee was charged.

cards.title: Success does not mean all of it arrived
cards.text: A payment can say tesSUCCESS and deliver a tiny part of its stated amount. Level 3 shows how, and what to check instead.

lessons.keyIdea: Only a result in a validated ledger is final. Read the metadata, not the request.

quiz.question: A result starts with tec. What happened?
options: It failed but was recorded, and the fee was charged
quiz.why: tec codes are recorded failures: nothing moved except the fee.

quiz.question: Where is a transaction's final result stored?
options: In its metadata, in a validated ledger
quiz.why: Metadata records what actually happened once the ledger is validated.

quiz.question: What happens to the small XRP fee every transaction pays?
quiz.why: The transaction cost is burned. That protects the network from spam without paying anyone.

lessons.title: Tokens, issuers and trust lines
goals: I can explain what a token and its issuer are.
I can say why a token's name proves nothing.

cards.title: Tokens are promises
cards.text: Besides XRP, the ledger carries tokens: digital dollars, euros, gold, shares. Every token is created by an issuer, an account that promises the token is backed by something. RLUSD, BBRL and AUDD are stablecoins issued this way.

cards.title: Trust lines
cards.text: To hold a token you open a trust line to its issuer. The trust line records the most you are willing to hold (the limit) and how much you hold now. Each trust line adds 0.2 XRP to your reserve.

cards.title: Think of it like
cards.text: A gift card. It is only worth something because the shop that issued it promises to honour it. A card with the same name from a different shop is a different card.

cards.title: The name proves nothing
cards.text: A token is identified by its currency code AND its issuer address. Anyone can issue a token called USD. Scammers send look-alike tokens to people's accounts. Always ask: who issued this?

lessons.keyIdea: Ask "who issued this?" before "what is it called?". The issuer address is the token's identity.

quiz.question: What identifies a token on the XRPL?
options: Its currency code and its issuer address together
quiz.why: Anyone can use the code USD. The issuer address is what makes it a specific token.

quiz.question: What must you open before you can hold a token?
options: A trust line to its issuer
quiz.why: A TrustSet transaction opens the trust line that records your limit and balance.

quiz.question: A stranger sends you 1,000 "USD" from an issuer you have never heard of. What should you think?
options: It may be a look-alike token; check the issuer
quiz.why: A familiar code from an unknown issuer is a classic impersonation. NOSHASHI's Inbox flags these.

lessons.title: What an issuer can still do
goals: I can name the issuer powers: freeze, clawback, Require Auth and transfer fee.
I can read an Authority verdict without treating it as an accusation.

cards.title: Powers live on the issuer's account
cards.text: Issuers can switch on powers stored as flags on their account. They are public, but almost no wallet shows them. They decide whether a token is really yours. This is the most important lesson in the course.

cards.title: Freeze
cards.text: An issuer can freeze one holder, or everyone at once (global freeze). A frozen holder can only send the token back to the issuer. An issuer that sets No Freeze gives up freezing forever.

cards.title: Clawback and Require Auth
cards.text: Clawback lets the issuer take tokens back out of your account. It can only be switched on before the issuer has any trust lines. Require Auth means you need the issuer's approval before you can hold the token.

cards.title: Transfer fee
cards.text: An issuer can charge a percentage every time holders send its token to each other, from 0% to 100%. The issuer can change it later.

cards.title: Real readings, 24 September 2026
cards.text: Bitstamp: freeze rights kept, one key can sign, 0.15% fee → NO-GO. Sologenic: No Freeze set, blackholed, 0.01% fee → HOLD. A NO-GO is not an accusation. Regulated issuers often must keep freeze rights. It tells you what they can still do.

lessons.keyIdea: A token can be yours on paper and still be frozen or taken back. Read the issuer's powers before you hold it.

quiz.question: What does clawback let an issuer do?
options: Take its tokens back out of a holder's account
quiz.why: Clawback lets the issuer recover tokens. It can only be enabled before any trust lines exist.

quiz.question: An issuer has set No Freeze. What does that mean?
options: It has given up freezing, permanently
It can freeze, but only on weekends
quiz.why: No Freeze can never be switched back off.

quiz.question: A well-known regulated issuer gets NO-GO. What is the best way to read that?
options: A fact about what the issuer can still do, not an accusation
Proof the issuer is a scam
quiz.why: NO-GO usually means one key can sign or freeze rights are kept. Many regulated issuers must keep them.

lessons.title: Who really controls an account
goals: I can name the three ways to sign for an account.
I can count a multi-signature quorum using weights, not headcount.

cards.title: Three ways to sign
cards.text: Master key: the original key. Regular key: a second key the account picks, handy for keeping the master offline. Signer list: up to 32 people, each with a weight. More than one can be active at once.

cards.title: Count weights, not people
cards.text: Alice 3, Bob 2, Carol 2, Dan 1, Eve 1. Quorum 5. Alice and Bob together have 3 + 2 = 5, so only two people are needed, not "three of five". NOSHASHI's Control Surface works this out for you.

cards.title: The master key can skip the list
cards.text: If the master key is still switched on, one person holding it can bypass the whole signer list. NOSHASHI flags this as a master-key bypass.

cards.title: Blackholed
cards.text: An account with its master key disabled, its regular key set to an address nobody can sign for, and no signer list is blackholed. Nobody can ever sign for it again. Its settings are frozen in time.

lessons.keyIdea: Count weights, not people, and check whether a master key can skip the whole process.

quiz.question: Weights: Alice 3, Bob 2, Carol 2. Quorum 5. What is the fewest people who can sign?
quiz.why: Alice (3) plus Bob or Carol (2) reaches 5.

quiz.question: A treasury has a signer list, but its master key is still enabled. What is the risk?
options: One person with the master key can bypass the list
quiz.why: An enabled master key can sign alone, skipping the signer list.

quiz.question: What does blackholed mean?
options: Nobody can ever sign for the account again
The account is frozen by Ripple
quiz.why: With no usable key and no signer list, nothing can change its settings or supply.

lessons.title: NFTs and the rights issuers keep
goals: I can say what an NFTokenID tells me.
I can name the rights an NFT issuer can keep.

cards.title: Unique tokens
cards.text: An NFT is a one-of-a-kind token: art, a ticket, a deed, a membership. Each has a 64-character NFTokenID. The ID itself holds the rules the issuer set when it was made.

cards.title: Rights an issuer can keep
cards.text: Burnable: the issuer can destroy it, even while you own it. Not transferable: you can only sell it back to the issuer. Mutable: the issuer can change what it points to. Transfer fee: up to 50% of every resale.

cards.title: No ledger call needed
cards.text: Because the rules are inside the ID, NOSHASHI's Token Rights screen can decode them straight from the 64 characters, without asking the ledger.

lessons.keyIdea: Owning an NFT does not mean the issuer is done with it. Its ID tells you what they kept.

quiz.question: Where are an NFT's rules stored?
options: In a PDF from the seller
quiz.why: The ID encodes the flags and the transfer fee the issuer set at minting.

quiz.question: What does mutable mean for an NFT?
options: The issuer can change what it points to after you buy it
It can be split into pieces
quiz.why: A mutable NFT's URI can change, so the picture or document can change.

quiz.question: What is the highest transfer fee an NFT issuer can set?
quiz.why: NFT transfer fees go up to 50%.

lessons.title: How the rules change
goals: I can explain how an amendment is switched on.

cards.title: Amendments
cards.text: The XRPL's rules change through amendments. A new feature is written into the server software, then validators vote. It switches on only after it keeps at least 80% support for two weeks in a row.

cards.title: Servers that fall behind
cards.text: A server that has not upgraded when an amendment switches on becomes amendment blocked. It stops following the ledger until it is upgraded.

cards.title: Features that arrived this way
cards.text: AMM pools (XLS-30), Clawback (XLS-39), NFTs (XLS-20), Credentials (XLS-70), Permissioned Domains (XLS-80) and Deep Freeze (XLS-77). An XLS number is the public proposal behind a feature.

lessons.keyIdea: New rules need a supermajority for two weeks. What is enabled today is readable from the ledger.

quiz.question: How does an amendment switch on?
options: 80% of validators support it for two weeks in a row
The first person to vote wins
quiz.why: It needs a supermajority that holds for two weeks.

quiz.question: What is an XLS number?
options: The public proposal behind a feature
quiz.why: For example, XLS-30 is the proposal for AMM pools.

quiz.question: What happens to a server that did not upgrade in time?
quiz.why: It stops following the ledger until it is upgraded.

lessons.title: Order books: listed versus funded
goals: I can explain what an order book is.
I can tell listed depth from funded depth.

cards.title: A built-in exchange
cards.text: The XRPL has had its own exchange, the DEX, since 2012. Anyone can post an offer, like "sell 100 USD for 190 XRP". All offers for one pair make an order book. The gap between the best buy and best sell is the spread.

cards.title: Some offers cannot trade
cards.text: An offer stays on the book even after its owner no longer has the money to fill it. It is still listed, but it cannot trade. These are unfunded offers.

cards.title: Worked example
cards.text: Three offers each list 10,000. Their owners hold 10,000, 500 and 0. Listed depth: 30,000. Funded depth: 10,500. Try to sell 20,000 and most of it will not fill.

cards.title: A real measurement, 8 September 2026
cards.text: USD from Bitstamp: listed and funded almost the same (1.0×). SOLO from Sologenic: listed 2,545 times what was funded. Deep stablecoin books are close to honest; the gap is in long-tail tokens. Re-measure before quoting: books change every few seconds.

lessons.keyIdea: Listed depth is an advert. Funded depth is what you can actually get out at.

quiz.question: Three offers list 10,000 each. Owners hold 10,000, 500 and 0. What is the funded depth?
quiz.why: Only what owners can actually deliver counts: 10,000 + 500 + 0.

quiz.question: What is an unfunded offer?
options: An offer still listed whose owner cannot fill it
quiz.why: It shows on the book but cannot trade.

quiz.question: Where is the gap between listed and funded depth usually largest?
quiz.why: In the September 2026 sample, stablecoin books were close to honest while SOLO and BTC were thousands of times overstated.

lessons.title: AMM pools
goals: I can explain what an AMM pool is and who governs its fee.

cards.title: A pool of two assets
cards.text: An automated market maker (AMM) is a pool holding two assets, for example XRP and a stablecoin. It trades with anyone at a price set by the ratio of the two balances. The DEX routes trades through books and pools, whichever is better.

cards.title: LP tokens
cards.text: People who deposit both assets get LP tokens: their share of the pool. Every swap pays a fee of up to 1% into the pool.

cards.title: Who sets the fee
cards.text: LP token holders vote on the fee, weighted by how many LP tokens they hold. Anyone can bid for the auction slot, which gives its holder much cheaper trades for a while.

cards.title: In NOSHASHI
cards.text: The Pool Governance screen shows who votes the fee, what share of LP tokens those votes carry, and who holds the auction slot. A pool whose fee is set by one big holder behaves differently from one with many voters.

lessons.keyIdea: A pool's fee and discounts are governed by whoever holds the most LP tokens. Check who that is.

quiz.question: What sets an AMM pool's price?
options: The ratio of the two balances in the pool
The last trade on another blockchain
quiz.why: The pool prices trades from the ratio of what it holds.

quiz.question: Who votes on a pool's trading fee?
options: LP token holders, weighted by their LP tokens
quiz.why: Voting power follows LP token holdings.

quiz.question: What does the auction slot give its holder?
options: Much cheaper trades for a while
The right to freeze the pool
quiz.why: The slot holder trades at a heavily discounted fee.

lessons.title: Payments: credit what arrived
goals: I can explain a partial payment.
I can say which figure to credit: delivered_amount.

cards.title: The Amount can lie
cards.text: A Payment's Amount says how much should arrive. If the sender sets the partial payment flag, the Amount is only a maximum. The payment can deliver far less and still say tesSUCCESS.

cards.title: Credit delivered_amount
cards.text: The true figure is delivered_amount, in the transaction's metadata. The XRPL's own documentation says to credit that. Exchanges that credited Amount instead have been drained.

cards.title: A real case, 28 August 2026
cards.text: Amount: 999,332.87 LRC. Delivered: 3,958.64 LRC, about 0.4%. Result: tesSUCCESS. A system crediting the Amount would have over-credited by about 250 times.

cards.title: Destination tags
cards.text: A destination tag is a number that tells a shared account, like an exchange, which customer a payment is for. A missing tag is a common reason a deposit seems lost.

lessons.keyIdea: Credit what was delivered, never what was asked for.

quiz.question: Which figure should you credit for a payment?
options: Whatever the sender says in an email
quiz.why: delivered_amount is what actually arrived.

quiz.question: Can a partial payment say tesSUCCESS and still deliver almost nothing?
quiz.why: In the real LRC case, about 0.4% arrived and the result was tesSUCCESS.

quiz.question: What is a destination tag for?
options: Telling a shared account which customer a payment is for
quiz.why: Exchanges and custodians use the tag to credit the right customer.

lessons.title: Did this payment pay this invoice?
goals: I can run an Invoice check and read VERIFIED, HOLD or REJECTED.
I can explain why the check compares exact amounts and reads two servers.

cards.title: The question a business really has
cards.text: Settlement tells you what a transaction moved. The Invoice check asks the next question: did this transaction pay this invoice? You enter the receiving account, an optional destination tag, the asset and the amount you expect.

cards.title: Three answers
cards.text: VERIFIED: it paid the invoice. HOLD: something needs a person to look, for example the ledger is not validated yet. REJECTED: it did not pay, with the reason in plain words. Only VERIFIED is green.

cards.title: Exact, and checked twice
cards.text: Amounts are compared exactly, digit by digit, never rounded. By default the check reads two independent node operators, XRPL Labs and Ripple, and says so if they disagree. Every answer comes with an evidence fingerprint (SHA-256).

cards.title: A real case on mainnet
cards.text: A CSC payment asked for 162.6994990013102 and delivered 161.1605415577872 (ledger 107,587,014). Expecting the full amount → REJECTED, partial not permitted. Expecting 161.1605415577872 with partial payments allowed → VERIFIED.

cards.title: Practise for free on testnet
cards.text: Testnet is a practice copy of the XRP Ledger where XRP has no value. The Invoice check has a TESTNET switch, and the testnet lab gives you real testnet payments to check.

lessons.keyIdea: An invoice is paid only by what was delivered, to the right account and tag, in a validated ledger.

quiz.question: Which answer means the invoice was paid?
quiz.why: Only VERIFIED is green. HOLD needs a person to look; REJECTED did not pay.

quiz.question: A payment delivered slightly less than the invoice, and partial payments are not allowed. What will the check say?
options: It rounds up and says VERIFIED
quiz.why: Amounts are exact. The real CSC case was REJECTED for exactly this reason.

quiz.question: What is testnet?
options: A practice copy of the XRP Ledger where XRP has no value
quiz.why: Testnet lets you practise with real transactions that cost nothing.

lessons.title: Compliance words, made simple
goals: I can explain KYC, AML, sanctions screening and the Travel Rule in my own words.
I can say what behaviour screening cannot see.

cards.title: Two questions
cards.text: Compliance means following the laws for moving money. On the XRPL it comes down to two questions. Am I allowed to move this? Could I actually get out of it? The first is law and policy. The second is market reality.

cards.title: The words
cards.text: KYC: checking who a customer is. AML: rules to stop criminal money. Sanctions screening: checking no one is on a government blocklist. Travel Rule: sender and receiver details travel with larger transfers between regulated firms.

cards.title: Travel Rule thresholds
cards.text: FATF suggests 1,000 USD or EUR. The US uses 3,000 USD. The EU applies it with no minimum. NOSHASHI lets you set your jurisdiction and tells you when a transfer is in scope.

cards.title: What screening misses
cards.text: Behaviour screening asks whether a person is risky. It cannot see what a token's issuer can do. A clean holder can hold a token that can be frozen or clawed back. NOSHASHI reads both sides.

cards.title: Compliance built into the ledger
cards.text: Credentials (XLS-70) let a trusted issuer, like a KYC provider, vouch for an account without revealing personal data. Permissioned domains (XLS-80) admit only accounts holding the right credentials.

lessons.keyIdea: Know who you deal with, know what the asset allows, and keep evidence you can show later.

quiz.question: What does KYC mean?
options: Know Your Customer: checking who a customer is
quiz.why: KYC is identity verification.

quiz.question: What can behaviour screening NOT see?
options: What a token's issuer can still do
quiz.why: Issuer powers are a property of the asset, stored in the issuer's flags.

quiz.question: What does a credential (XLS-70) let an issuer do?
options: Vouch for an account without revealing personal data
quiz.why: That is selective disclosure: proof without the underlying data.

lessons.title: What NOSHASHI is, and how it reads
goals: I can describe NOSHASHI's two questions.
I can list how NOSHASHI keeps its readings honest.

cards.title: Both questions, one reading
cards.text: NOSHASHI is a desktop app for macOS, Windows and Linux. It answers both compliance questions about any account, token, pool or payment: am I allowed to move this, and could I get out of it? It reads both from the same ledger reading.

cards.title: How it stays honest
cards.text: It reads validated ledgers only. It compares several public servers and shows any disagreement. When it cannot tell, it says so instead of showing zero. It never asks for keys, never signs and never moves money.

cards.title: Stamped and fingerprinted
cards.text: Every result carries the ledger index it was read at and a SHA-256 digest: a fingerprint of the exact result. Change one character and the fingerprint changes completely.

cards.title: Who uses it
cards.text: Compliance officers, trading desks, treasury teams, token issuers and auditors. And anyone checking an address before paying it, for free.

lessons.keyIdea: Validated only, compared across servers, honest about unknowns, and never holding keys.

quiz.question: What are NOSHASHI's two questions?
options: Am I allowed to move this? Could I actually get out of it?
What is the price? Should I buy?
Who is the CEO? Where is the office?
quiz.why: Law and policy on one side, market reality on the other.

quiz.question: What does NOSHASHI do when the ledger does not give enough to decide?
options: Says so, instead of guessing or showing zero
quiz.why: It withholds the figure and explains why.

quiz.question: What is a SHA-256 digest?
options: A fingerprint of the exact result
quiz.why: Change one character of the result and the digest changes completely.

lessons.title: Verdicts, checks and receipts
goals: I can explain GO, HOLD and NO-GO.
I can name the five states a check can report.

cards.title: Three verdicts
cards.text: GO: every check passed. HOLD: a warning-level check did not pass, or something needs review; a person should look before moving. NO-GO: a blocking check failed; do not move until it is resolved or formally excepted.

cards.title: Five check states
cards.text: PASS: run and satisfied. FAIL: run and not satisfied. REVIEW: needs a human decision. INSUFFICIENT_DATA: not enough to decide, never counted as a pass. NOT_APPLICABLE: the check does not apply.

cards.title: The receipt
cards.text: Every verdict makes a receipt: what was checked, the ledger index, the rules version, each check's result and a SHA-256 digest over all of it. Anyone who recomputes the digest over the same contents gets the same value.

cards.title: Your policy
cards.text: Your organisation can tune checks with its own thresholds and required credentials. A verdict says when a policy was applied, or that it shows raw ledger facts only.

lessons.keyIdea: Read the verdict, then open the checks: every result names the exact rule that decided it.

quiz.question: A blocking check failed. What is the verdict?
quiz.why: Any failed blocking check gives NO-GO.

quiz.question: Is INSUFFICIENT_DATA a pass?
quiz.why: Not enough data never counts as passing.

quiz.question: What lets someone check later that a receipt was not altered?
quiz.why: The same contents always give the same digest; any change gives a different one.

lessons.title: A tour of the app
goals: I can find any screen in the sidebar and say what it is for.
I can start with Mission Control and Check an Address.

cards.title: Start here
cards.text: Open Mission Control first. If the ledger number climbs every few seconds, you are connected and current. If it stops, readings will be stale until it resumes.

cards.title: Am I allowed to move this?
cards.text: Verification runs a settlement through the gate. Provenance shows how old a counterparty is and who funded it. Credentials and Domain Grid show who vouched for an account and where it is admitted.

cards.title: Could I get out of it?
cards.text: Order Book shows funded depth. Pool Governance shows who controls an AMM. Exposure Analysis puts a position's risks together. Portfolio & Radar watches many wallets at once.

cards.title: Treasury, issuance and records
cards.text: Control Surface shows who can move a treasury. Issuance, Authority and Passport describe a token from the issuer's side. Audit Trail and Settlement read history and payments. Ledger & Policy keeps your verdicts and exports.

cards.title: Free tools
cards.text: Check an Address (10 a month), Inbox (claims sent to you), Token Rights (NFTs), Ledger Sync (what four servers say) and the Security Center's free tools work without a paid plan.

lessons.keyIdea: Mission Control first, then the screen that answers your question. Buttons say READING… while they work.

quiz.question: Which screen should you glance at first to confirm you are connected?
quiz.why: A climbing ledger number means a live, current connection.

quiz.question: Which screen tells you how old a counterparty is and who funded it?
quiz.why: Provenance traces an account's real age and first funder.

quiz.question: Which screen shows who can move a treasury?
quiz.why: Control Surface reads the master key, signer list and minimum signers.

lessons.title: Teams, policies and the Agent
goals: I can explain four-eyes approval and why investigations are hash-chained.
I can say what the Agent is for, and what it is not.

cards.title: Four-eyes policy
cards.text: An organisation shares one policy. A change starts as a draft, can be simulated against past verdicts, and needs a second person to approve it before it is active. Every step is logged.

cards.title: Exceptions and investigations
cards.text: A NO-GO can be overridden only through an exception a reviewer approves, possibly after asking for evidence. An investigation (a case) collects readings and notes. Its log is hash-chained, so entries cannot be quietly edited.

cards.title: The Agent
cards.text: The Agent is an AI assistant in the app. By default it runs on your own computer, so nothing leaves it. It explains readings, helps with the app, and the Observer watches issuers and wallets for changes.

cards.title: Use it wisely
cards.text: The Agent explains; the ledger decides. Always confirm important points against the readings and receipts themselves.

lessons.keyIdea: Two people approve rule changes, every decision is logged, and the ledger, not the AI, decides.

quiz.question: What is four-eyes approval?
options: A second person must approve a policy change
quiz.why: One person drafts, another approves; both are logged.

quiz.question: Why is an investigation's log hash-chained?
options: So entries cannot be quietly edited or removed
quiz.why: Each entry includes the fingerprint of the one before.

quiz.question: The Agent and a ledger reading disagree. Which do you trust?
quiz.why: The Agent explains; the ledger decides.

lessons.title: Making an account hard to take over
goals: I can list the four defences for an account.
I can explain address poisoning and how to avoid it.

cards.title: How accounts get emptied
cards.text: Nobody can reset an XRPL account or undo a payment. Most accounts are emptied because the secret was exposed: typed into a fake site, saved in a cloud note or screenshot, or read by malware. The ledger itself is not broken into.

cards.title: Four defences
cards.text: 1. Keep the master seed offline, on paper or steel. 2. Sign day to day with a regular key in a hardware wallet. 3. Require several signers for a treasury, then disable the master key. 4. Close doors strangers use, like unsolicited offers and checks.

cards.title: Address poisoning, a real example
cards.text: The account rfWPjcbY5QT2shRFY2SSQHFKPYSMzxaMaN sent 1-drop payments with a fake "free XRP" link, then deleted itself into the next account. Each account was made to end in "xaman", the name of a real wallet.

cards.title: The habit that beats poisoning
cards.text: Take addresses from your own saved records, never from your transaction history. The Security Center's free SAFE SEND names any look-alike of an address you have paid before.

lessons.keyIdea: Your account is exactly as safe as the least protected key that can sign for it.

quiz.question: How are most XRPL accounts emptied?
quiz.why: Fake sites, cloud notes, screenshots and malware expose secrets.

quiz.question: What is address poisoning?
options: Sending you a tiny payment from a look-alike address so you copy it later
quiz.why: The fake sits next to the real address in your history.

quiz.question: Where should you copy a payee's address from?
quiz.why: History is exactly where poisoned look-alikes appear.

lessons.title: When an account is emptied
goals: I can list what to do in the first hour after a theft.
I can spot a fake recovery service.

cards.title: The hard truth first
cards.text: A validated XRPL payment is final. Nobody can reverse it: not validators, not Ripple, not wallet makers, not NOSHASHI. Anyone offering to recover stolen XRP for a fee is running the second half of the scam.

cards.title: The first hour
cards.text: Move anything left to a brand-new account made on a clean device. Check whether the thief added their own keys. Follow where the value went. Report it to the police with transaction hashes, amounts and times; in the US that is ic3.gov.

cards.title: Paths that can work
cards.text: An exchange can freeze a deposit if reached quickly, usually with a police reference. A token's issuer can freeze, or claw back, stolen tokens unless it gave that up. Authorities can act when a trail reaches a sanctioned address.

cards.title: In NOSHASHI
cards.text: Incident Response follows the value hop by hop, past dust and deleted accounts, says where it is now, rates each recovery path honestly, and writes a fingerprinted dossier for police, exchanges and issuers.

lessons.keyIdea: Nothing reverses a validated payment. Speed, evidence and the right request to the right party are what recover funds, when anything can.

quiz.question: Someone offers to reverse your stolen XRP for a fee. What is it?
quiz.why: Validated payments cannot be reversed by anyone.

quiz.question: What should you do first?
options: Move what is left to a new account made on a clean device
Post your seed online for help
quiz.why: Whoever has the old key can take the rest at any moment.

quiz.question: Who can sometimes freeze stolen funds?
options: An exchange that received them, or the token's issuer
quiz.why: Custodians and issuers with freeze rights are the realistic paths.

lessons.title: Getting XRP back, and signing safely
goals: I can name kinds of stuck XRP that can be recovered.
I can name the signatures that empty accounts.

cards.title: XRP you can get back
cards.text: A matured escrow waits for someone to finish it. A check written to you pays nothing until you cash it. Every object you own locks 0.2 XRP; removing ones you no longer need frees it.

cards.title: Real examples from mainnet
cards.text: Ripple's escrow wallet #03 (rB3WNZc45gxzW31zxfXdkx8HusAhoqscPn) holds ten escrows to itself, waiting to be finished. An NFT trader had four expired buy offers: 0.8 XRP of reserve returns when they are cancelled.

cards.title: Read before you sign
cards.text: A phishing site does not need your seed if you will sign for it. Dangerous signatures: SetRegularKey or SignerListSet (hand over control), AccountDelete (sends everything away), and an NFT offer for zero.

cards.title: Is this account who it says?
cards.text: Anyone can write a domain on an account. It is proven only when that website lists the account in its xrp-ledger.toml file. The Security Center's free DOMAIN CHECK tests this.

lessons.keyIdea: Nobody can reverse a theft, but you can finish, cancel, cash and clean up what is yours, and refuse to sign what you have not read.

quiz.question: An escrow has matured. Does the XRP move by itself?
quiz.why: Escrows wait for a finishing transaction.

quiz.question: Which signature can hand control of your account to someone else?
options: Payment of 1 XRP to a friend
quiz.why: SetRegularKey and SignerListSet give signing power away.

quiz.question: An account's Domain says bitstamp.net. Is it proven?
options: Only if bitstamp.net lists it in its xrp-ledger.toml
Yes, if the account is old
quiz.why: Anyone can write a domain; the website must list the account back.

lessons.title: Protecting customers' XRP
goals: I can explain proof of reserves and why liabilities matter too.
I can tell a real protection fund from one that counts for nothing.

cards.title: Reserves AND liabilities
cards.text: A big balance proves little if the business owes more. A Merkle sum tree proves what a business owes all customers without showing anyone's balance. Each customer can check they are counted.

cards.title: A real tree
cards.text: Built over the 138 holders of a real token (USDB), the tree totals exactly what the ledger says the issuer owes: 33,733,671.32 USDB. Understate one holder and their path no longer reaches the root.

cards.title: A fund no single key can move
cards.text: Locked in escrow until a date: strong. Under a signer list with the master key disabled: strong. Behind one key: whoever holds it can take it, so it counts for nothing.

cards.title: Verification, not insurance
cards.text: NOSHASHI shows what is really set aside. It pays no claims, and no government scheme stands behind it.

lessons.keyIdea: A promise about customers' XRP is worth what the ledger can show.

quiz.question: Why are reserves alone not enough?
options: The business might owe customers more than it holds
quiz.why: You need liabilities too, to work out coverage.

quiz.question: A protection fund sits behind one key. How much does it count for?
options: Nothing, whoever holds the key can take it
quiz.why: Only escrow or a real signer list makes a fund hard to take.

quiz.question: Is NOSHASHI's protection view insurance?
quiz.why: It shows what is set aside; it does not pay claims.
